title: The Apostles' Creed, line by line
hookLine: twelve lines, from creator to life everlasting
last: AS IT WAS IN THE BEGINNING.

lines: I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE. I BELIEVE.
cards: Rome, in the early Church, as an old church order describes it. It's the night before Easter, in the dark. A woman stands waist-deep in water.
A church leader asks her: do you believe in God, the Father almighty? She says: I believe. And she's plunged under.
Do you believe in Christ Jesus, the Son of God? I believe. Under again.
Do you believe in the Holy Spirit, and the holy Church? I believe. Under a third time, and up, and she's a Christian.

teach.b: Creed comes from the Latin credo: I believe. The Apostles' Creed opens in Latin: Credo in Deum, Patrem omnipotentem, Creatorem caeli et terrae. I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.
Then it moves like a story. Jesus Christ, his only Son. Conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.
Suffered under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He descended to the dead, rose on the third day, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead.
Then the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting. Notice Pontius Pilate.
Besides Jesus and Mary, the one person the creed names is a Roman governor. It pins the whole thing to a real time and place. Why the Apostles'?

teach.h: A LEGEND, AND A SLOWER HISTORY.
teach.b: An old legend, written down around the year 400, says the twelve apostles each gave one line before they went out into the world.
Historians say it grew more slowly, from those baptism questions in Rome, reaching its present shape centuries later. The Church uses it either way, as a faithful summary of what the apostles taught.
And credo isn't a list of opinions. Some linguists connect it with an ancient root that may mean to put your heart. To believe, in this old sense, isn't to hold a fact in your head.
It's to set your heart on something, and lean your weight there.

how: Catholics pray the Apostles' Creed at the start of the rosary and at baptisms, and it may replace the longer Nicene Creed at Sunday Mass, especially in Lent and the Easter season.

games.q: Rome, in the early Church, the night before Easter. you're standing in the water to be baptized. what happens?
o: you recite a long creed from memory.
you're asked three questions, and answer I believe to each.
you sign a written statement of faith.
games.why: three questions, about the Father, the Son and the Spirit, and three times under the water. those questions grew into the Apostles' Creed.

practice: If you know the Apostles' Creed by heart, say it in your mind one line at a time, with a breath after each line, and don't rush to the end.

If you don't know it, take just the first line, I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth, and sit with it. Whether you believe it or not, notice what it would mean to lean your weight there.

wordCard.voice: Creed. From credo, I believe: a short statement of faith, with roots in questions asked at baptism.

orig.note: Latin: I believe, the first word of the creed and the root of the English word.

carryVoice: Your line: I believe is a verb. Three answers in the water became twelve lines. That's day one hundred and one.
